props.title: My Name Is Bill W.

sections.content: My Name Is Bill W. stands as one of the most powerful addiction recovery films ever made, anchored by James Woods' raw portrayal of Alcoholics Anonymous co-founder Bill Wilson. The film unfolds during the Great Depression, tracking Wilson's descent from successful stockbroker to desperate alcoholic, before showing his transformative friendship with Dr. Bob Smith (James Garner) that led to AA's creation. Unlike glossier addiction films like Clean and Sober (1988) or 28 Days (2000), this made-for-TV masterpiece maintains documentary-like authenticity while dramatizing pivotal moments in recovery movement history.

sections.content: The film's greatest strength lies in how it depicts the development of AA's core principles through Wilson's personal journey. We see the birth of concepts like powerlessness over alcohol, the importance of peer support, and the spiritual component of recovery emerging organically from Wilson's experiences. Clean and Sober (1988) and Leaving Las Vegas (1995) may offer more stylized portraits of addiction, but My Name Is Bill W. shows the raw humanity behind recovery's fundamental building blocks.

The period setting proves crucial, as the film illustrates how the Depression era's widespread desperation created fertile ground for AA's message. Director Daniel Petrie captures both the external chaos of the stock market crash and the internal turmoil of addiction without sensationalism. This approach influenced later recovery-themed films like When Love Is Not Enough: The Lois Wilson Story (2010), which explores AA's impact from the perspective of Bill's wife. sections.content: My Name Is Bill W. helped establish a template for honest portrayals of addiction and recovery that influenced countless later works. Films like Beautiful Boy (2018) and Ben Is Back (2018) follow its lead in examining addiction's impact on families, while Thanks for Sharing (2012) applies similar themes to other forms of addiction. The film's emphasis on hope and transformation, without minimizing addiction's brutal reality, remains its most lasting contribution to the genre.
